items.exp_text: A constellation is an area on the celestial sphere in which a group of visible stars forms a perceived pattern or outline. The pattern often represents an animal, a mythological subject, or an inanimate object. The stars in that area are not necessarily close to each other in space; they just appear close in the sky.

items.exp_text: The word constellation comes from the Late Latin term cōnstellātiō, which can be translated as 'set of stars'. It came into use in Middle English during the 14th century. The term refers to a group of stars seen as a pattern, not to any single star or shape.

items.exp_text: An asterism is a star pattern or group that is used by observers to navigate the night sky, but it is not a constellation under the formal definition. Asterisms can be several stars within one constellation, or they can share stars with more than one constellation. Examples include the Teapot in Sagittarius and the Big Dipper in Ursa Major.

items.prompt: What does it mean for a constellation to be circumpolar?

options.label: It never sets below the horizon when viewed from a particular latitude
options.feedback: Yes, a circumpolar constellation or star never sets below the horizon for that latitude.

options.label: It is always visible from every place on Earth
options.feedback: Circumpolarity depends on latitude; a constellation may be circumpolar from one latitude but not from another.

options.label: It is the same as a zodiac constellation
options.feedback: Circumpolarity is about visibility, not about being in the zodiac.

options.label: It is a constellation that contains the pole star
options.feedback: A circumpolar constellation does not need to contain the pole star; it just never sets.

items.ok_line: Circumpolar means never setting below the horizon at that latitude.
items.ko_line: Circumpolar refers to not setting, not to being zodiacal or containing a pole star.
items.exp_text: A constellation or star that never sets below the horizon when viewed from a particular latitude on Earth is termed circumpolar. From the North Pole or South Pole, all constellations south or north of the celestial equator are circumpolar. Depending on the definition, equatorial constellations may include those that lie between declinations 45° north and 45° south.

items.exp_text: Sigma Octantis is the closest star approximating a southern pole star, but it is faint in the night sky. Because it is dim, the southern pole is often found using the constellation Crux and the stars Alpha and Beta Centauri, which are about 30° counterclockwise from Crux.
